Active-sensing blood pressure ring

One ring, three sensors, the KavAI world model that decides when to look closer

Part 1

The ring

A 3D model built from the real part sizes. A band 8 mm wide and 2.3 to 2.6 mm thick carries three blood pressure sensors, repeated in four sectors, with the battery, radio and charging coil. The model shows the 8 mm study; revision D, the prototype design, is 8.6 mm wide.

What the model settles

  • It fits at ring sizes 9 to 13. At sizes 6 to 8 the two palm-side islands are up to 1.5 mm too long for the space between the core and the side tiles.
  • The battery is the tightest volume. Two arcs, each 12.2 x 5.5 x 1.4 mm at size 10, hold 85 mWh at 450 Wh/L. This model shows the 8.0 mm study. Revision D widens the shell to 8.6 mm and its cell gives 37.9 mWh usable at size 9 when aged, which is what the battery figure uses. Vendor quotes confirm it.
  • The charging coil faces the finger side, on the inner face of the battery. Titanium blocks the charging field, so the charger has to be a post that goes through the ring.
  • Sector 1 sits 13 degrees off the palm centre, because the core is two halves and the sensors are in one of them.
  • Not modelled: potting, the weld or bond of the shell, solder joints, and the bend of the flex at each rigid part.

Part 2

Why this design

Optical wearables estimate blood pressure from light and drift back toward their last cuff reading. Fixing that takes sensors that see the artery, and those are expensive to run.

The hard part is not the sensors. It is deciding when to use them.

PPG alone is cheap but not accurate. The laser and ultrasound are accurate but cost 10 to 50 times more power. The KavAI model runs PPG all the time and switches the costly sensors on only when they are needed. Power figures are from the per-component power model, ahead of bench measurement.

Three sensors, three jobs

Always on

PPG

Green, red and infrared light. Cheap, so it runs all the time at low power and low resolution as the change detector.

On demand

Laser speckle

An 850 nm laser sees blood flow in the small vessels. Medium cost. It carries most of the accuracy.

Rarely

Ultrasound

A 12 MHz array sees the artery itself: diameter and wall motion. The most expensive. Meant to locate the artery and recalibrate the optical sensors.

What each sensor buys

Systolic error spread in the ring simulator. Shorter is better. Laser speckle is essential. In simulation ultrasound changes the result little: its role is recalibration over weeks, which bench data will show.

ISO 81060-2 limit: a spread of 8 mmHg

Anyone can put three sensors in a band. The advantage is the KavAI world model that decides what to measure, when, and how sure it is.

imec has the speckle optics, the transducer process and the fab, so the parts are not what sets this apart. Four things the KavAI model does, with the next step for each.

1 · Power

Spends energy on questions

1.28 mW for −1.0 ± 7.7 mmHg. A fixed timer with the same energy gets −1.3 ± 8.5, outside the ISO limit.

Next: widen the 0.58 mmHg lead. Today it runs a scheduled baseline plus event-triggered checks, with costly readings 12% more frequent when pressure is moving.

2 · Anomaly calling

Names what changed

The firmware's sequential tests name device artifacts (band shift, temperature, poor contact) 99 to 100% of the time. Night-time hypertension is caught 86% of the time.

Next: sudden 20 mmHg rises are caught 43% of the time (46% for a timer) with about 8 false alarms a day. Change detection tuned on bench data is the main work item; clinical alerts follow its validation.

3 · Honest confidence

Knows what it doesn't know

Every reading carries a range. After calibration the 95% range holds the truth 94.9% of the time. If the reasoning layer fails, a reflex layer takes over and labels its output.

Next: per-wearer ranges. For the hardest 5% of wearers the range holds 77% today.

4 · Learning

Learns each wearer

Every costly reading is logged with its reason and its energy. That log is the training set and the regulatory record at once. A month later the ring still reads within the same error with no cuff.

Next: move the per-wearer cuff update from simulation into firmware. The design reduces cuff calibration; it does not remove it.

Part 3

How it works

Cheap sensing runs all the time. A small model on the ring predicts what it should see next and switches on the costly sensors only when it has to.

Where the sensors sit

The two finger arteries run along the palm side. A ring rotates, so the sensor trio is repeated in four sectors and the model learns which one faces an artery.

What is in the package

How the KavAI model steps up the sensors

PPG watches at half a milliwatt. The model steps up one level at a time: full PPG, a low-resolution laser check, full-resolution laser, then an ultrasound burst.

The layers

  • Safety supervisorA separate small processor. It grants every laser and ultrasound shot and can only veto. Nothing above can override it.
  • L3 · reasoningBeliefs, seven hypotheses, sequential tests, and the choice of the next measurement by information per millijoule.
  • L2 · salienceChange detection on the model's surprise.
  • L1 · reflexMotion, band shift, contact and a fallback estimate. Must work alone.
  • L0 · driversSensors, radio, power rails, with energy metered per action.
  • Sleep · phoneNightly model updates, signed, with rollback protection.

What runs on the ring

  • The whole model fits on the radio chip. 30,285 parameters, 118 kB, about 30 thousand multiply-accumulates every 2 seconds.
  • Firmware is C99 with no heap, one module per layer. It matches the Python reference on 5,400 of 5,400 sensing decisions, and 84 host checks pass.
  • Signal processing sits on the sensor chips. Speckle contrast and artery-wall tracking are specified on the custom chips, so the radio chip's 256 kB of RAM holds only the model and the control code. That signal-processing code is the next to be tested.
  • The safety supervisor has its own processor in the circuit. Its firmware is tested on the host and is ported to that processor next.

Part 5

Electronics

Revision D is the prototype circuit: drawn in KiCad, rule-checked, placed and routed on the ring's flex board at all five sizes.

Circuit, revision D

416 parts

11 schematic sheets; the KiCad netlist matches the design source

Board layout

0 errors

KiCad design-rule check at sizes US 9 to 13, every net routed, on the 7.0 mm board

Custom silicon

3 chips

speckle imager, ultrasound tile front end and receiver, plus the transducer, specified for imec

Bluetooth

+8 dBm

transmit power, with the antenna match set for the 8.6 mm shell. Confirmed on the first worn rings

Power tree

One always-on 1.8 V rail keeps the watch level at about half a milliwatt. The 1.2 V, 3.0 V, 4.3 V, 2.8 V and 24 V rails are off until the world model escalates. Laser, LED, ultrasound and 24 V rails each have a shunt read by the ADC while on, so the energy of each action is metered.

Path to hardware

  • Bench rig first. It measures the speckle, PPG and ultrasound coupling the accuracy figures assume. The laser limit resistor is set from the measured curve of the actual laser before it is powered.
  • Then the revision D ring boards. The layout is released for sizes US 9 to 13. Antenna match and charge time are confirmed on the first assembled rings.
  • imec builds the custom chips and the transducer from the specifications in the project files.

Battery mode

Cuff check-in

Removed in this version. The firmware did not apply cuff readings, so the old screen said "offset applied" when nothing happened. A per-wearer update that models the cuff's own error is designed and simulated, not yet in firmware or validated.

Connect a ring

Uses Bluetooth LE. The live characteristic sends 14 bytes every 2 seconds.

Prototype for engineering evaluation. Not a medical device. Do not use these numbers to make treatment decisions. This prototype raises no clinical alerts: the alerts are defined in the risk file and are not implemented or validated.

Part 7

Status and next steps

What the design assumes, and the steps from here to a working prototype.

Assumptions to confirm

  • Speckle signal strength of 0.75. The accuracy figures depend on it. The bench rig measures it on 24 volunteers.
  • Power per sensing level. From a per-component model built on datasheet values. The first boards meter each rail.
  • Transducer output and sensitivity at 12 MHz. The ultrasound link budget uses imec's figures once measured.
  • The curved cell. 37.9 mWh usable at size US 9 when aged, charged to 4.45 V. Confirmed with two vendor quotes.
  • Cuff readings in week one. The spot-reading accuracy figure uses at least six.

What happens next

  • Build the bench rig and measure what the simulator assumes.
  • Get imec's answers on the ultrasound transducer, the speckle imager and the custom chips.
  • Build the revision D ring boards and bring up the laser safety chain on the bench.
  • Make the controller react to real change and put the per-wearer update in firmware.
  • Regulatory and clinical work: pre-submission, risk and usability files, ISO 81060 and ESH tests.

Expert review

54 defects found

51 apply to the ring: 24 fixed, 26 partly fixed, 1 open. Fixed means changed and checked in simulation. Four wiring corrections found while drawing the KiCad version are in revision D.

Expert panel review · bp-audit/v2/FIX_LOG.md

Bench rig, the first thing to build

20 pass marks

A rig from 41 catalogue parts (about €84k, estimated) measures speckle, PPG and ultrasound coupling on 24 volunteers. The pass marks are fixed before any data and decide whether the ring keeps each sensor. The design is complete; building it is the next step.
